notes.meaning: After two tries, Balaam finally understood that God was set on blessing Israel. So he stopped using the magic charms and signs he had tried before. He saw that they did him no good against God's plan. He simply turned to face the wilderness, where Israel was camped.

Balaam looked out and saw Israel's huge camp, set out in neat order, tribe by tribe. Then the Spirit of God came on him. This was the Spirit giving him a message from God, as once happened to King Saul (1 Samuel 19). From here on Balaam spoke God's words, not his own ideas.

Balaam opens with a solemn introduction. He calls himself a man who hears God's words and sees visions from the Almighty. Several commentators think the word for "open" in verse 3 may really mean "closed." If so, his outward eyes were shut while the eyes of his mind were opened to see God's vision. Some hear pride in these words, while others say their main point is that the message truly came from God. Matthew Henry adds a warning: many people have their eyes opened to truth while their hearts stay closed.

Balaam bursts out in praise of Israel's tents. They were plain, worn tents, not palaces. Yet they looked beautiful because they were set out in such good order and unity. Seen from the hills above, the great camp spread across the plain must have been a stunning sight.

Israel is pictured as green valleys, gardens by a river, sweet-smelling aloe trees and tall cedars by the water. These pictures show beauty, fruitfulness and lasting strength. Trees "the LORD has planted" means trees grown by God's own hand, finer than anything people could plant. Israel's beauty comes from God, who planted them.

Water overflowing from buckets is a picture of rich blessing, since water was precious in that hot land. "His seed" means Israel's children, who would grow many. "Agag" was probably a title for all the kings of Amalek, the way "Pharaoh" was used in Egypt. Israel's king would rise higher than these powerful enemy kings. Many see this coming true in David's kingdom and fully in the Messiah, God's promised Savior King.

Balaam looks back to how God Himself brought Israel out of Egypt with great power. Israel is now as strong as a wild ox that no one can tame. He also looks ahead. Israel will overcome the nations that fight against them. The God who brought them out of Egypt will surely bring them into their land.

Israel is like a lion lying down to rest, and no one dares to disturb it. This repeats words from Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49:9). The last line repeats God's promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3). God counts any kindness or harm done to His people as done to Himself. Some commentators also see here the victories of Jesus, the Lion of the tribe of Judah.

Balak is furious. Striking his hands together was a sign of great anger and of sending someone away in disgrace. He orders Balaam to go home. He mockingly blames God: "I would have rewarded you, but your LORD kept it from you." In this way he puts the blame on God for his own broken promise.

Balaam reminds Balak of what he said from the start. Not even a palace full of silver and gold could make him go beyond what God commanded. Balak had been fairly warned. Calvin notes that Balaam spoke the truth but seemed sorry to lose the reward, as if he obeyed because he had to, not gladly.

Before leaving, Balaam offers to tell Balak what Israel will do to Moab "in the days to come." The word for "warn" can also mean "advise." Some commentators link this to the evil advice Balaam later gave: to lead Israel into idol worship (Numbers 31:16; Revelation 2:14). Others take it more simply as a message that carried advice on how Balak should treat Israel.

Balaam starts his last prophecy with the same solemn opening. This time he adds that he has "knowledge from the Most High." Matthew Henry warns that a person can know a lot about God and speak of Him with great honor, yet not truly love, trust or fear Him. Knowing about God is not the same as having His grace.

Balaam sees someone far off in the future, "not now" and "not near." A star and a scepter (a king's rod) are pictures of a great king. This points first to David, who defeated Moab (2 Samuel 8:2). Above all it points to Jesus, the Messiah, whose rule reaches over the whole world. "Sons of Sheth" is unclear. It may mean all people, or it may be a name for Moab's warlike people. Some think this prophecy, kept alive in the East, helped lead the wise men to follow the star to Jesus (Matthew 2:2). Other commentators doubt that link.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read the star and scepter as pointing only to David, or to Israel's kings, and not to the Messiah.

notes.meaning: Edom, also called Seir after its mountains, would be taken over by Israel. This began when David conquered Edom (2 Samuel 8:14). Commentators say it will be fully true only when Christ overcomes all His enemies. Meanwhile Israel would grow strong and act bravely.

A ruler will come from Jacob's family. This is David, and especially Christ. He will not only win in open battle but will chase his enemies even into their strong cities. No stubborn enemy will escape.

Amalek is called "first among the nations." This may mean they were the first to attack Israel after Egypt (Exodus 17), or that they were proud of being old and powerful. Either way, their end would be destruction. This began under Saul and David and was finished in Hezekiah's day, when Amalek disappeared as a people.

The Kenites, relatives of Moses' father-in-law Jethro, seemed very safe, like a bird's nest high on a cliff. There is a play on words here, since "Kenite" sounds like the word for "nest." Yet they would slowly weaken until Assyria carried them off as captives. Some read it more hopefully: the Kenites would last until Assyria came. Matthew Henry draws the lesson that even a nest in a rock is no lasting safety without God.

Balaam cries out with sorrow at what he sees coming. "Who can live?" may mean these events are so far off that no one now alive will see them. Or it may mean the times will be so terrible that few will survive. Either way, he admits that God is the one behind the rise and fall of nations.

Ships from the west, from the direction of Cyprus, will bring down Assyria and Eber. Many understand these sea powers as Greece under Alexander and later Rome. "Eber" is often taken to mean the Hebrews, though some read it as other peoples beyond the Euphrates River. In the end even these conquerors will perish forever. Every worldly power falls in turn, but God's kingdom remains.

Balaam and Balak part ways, their plan to curse Israel a failure. Balaam set out for home, but later he was with the Midianites, gave his evil advice and was killed by Israel (Numbers 31:8). Calvin notes how God scatters the schemes of the wicked like clouds. Israel was later told to remember this rescue (Micah 6:5).
